transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-17 11:00 PST
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonah (Redwood SE), Priya R. (Redwood), Arjun (CTO - LumenPay), Sofia (Lead SRE), Daniel (ML Eng), Priya K. (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, low confidence): quick throughput check; dropped p99 spikes traced to cold kv-cache and two hot endpoints; tried lower concurrency + larger continuous batch for better throughput; agreed to steady-state run and share artifacts.

Topics: throughput numbers, continuous batching tradeoffs, concurrency targets, queue depth/backpressure, kv cache warmup, burst fallback policy, routing to dedicated pool suggestion.

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Maya: okay hi everyone, thanks for joining. we wanted to kick off with the lab results you ran yesterday at 3am, is that the one, Arjun?
[00:12] Arjun: yeah that was the one. we pushed a synthetic load around your earlier recommended qps and then bumped batch window up to 40ms, um, and saw some interesting numbers.
[00:26] Jonah: great, can you run us through the top-line? before we dig in into the p99 tails.
[00:31] Daniel: sure. so top-line, with continuous batching window 40ms, concurrency set to 8 per shard, we hit about 26k tokens/sec aggregate across two shards. average latency was around 160ms per request (1-2 token prompts), p95 was 220ms, p99 had spikes to 1.2s during cold-yellow periods.
[00:49] Sofia: cold-yellow? what does that mean, you mean when kv cache was cold?
[00:53] Daniel: yeah exactly. when a large fraction of requests missed the K-V cash — the transcriber had it as K-V cash which was funny — miss rate triggered longer decoding and we got those p99 spikes.
[01:06] Maya: okay that's consistent with what we've seen. continuous batching increases throughput but can amplify cold-cache tail if requests have diverse prompt prefixes.
[01:15] Priya R.: did you try the smaller window? last week we recommended 20ms then 40ms for throughput.
[01:20] Daniel: we ran 20ms as well; throughput dropped to about 19k tokens/sec but p99 tightened to around 480ms. so it's a tradeoff.
[01:29] Jonah: right — classic latency vs cost/throughput. one thing we haven't tried in this run is a small concurrency cap with a larger batch window plus aggressive kv-cache prefetch. that often gives a good middle ground.
[01:43] Arjun: what do you mean by prefetch? like pre-populate the kv cache with hot prefixes?
[01:47] Jonah: yeah, exactly. a warmup pass for top X prefixes you expect. we can also set an adaptive policy where requests that miss are routed to a less-batched path temporarily to avoid tail amplification.
[01:58] Sofia: is that the routing you were talking about — the fall-through to a lower-batch or even single-shot path? that could blow cost though.
[02:05] Maya: there's a couple of levers. we can do a hybrid where misses go to a low-latency pool and hits stay in continuous-batch. Redwood's runtime supports that via routing policy; it's a config flag plus an eval of how often we miss.
[02:18] Daniel: the miss rate at peak was about 14%. so if we route misses to low-batch path, cost goes up maybe 5-7% but p99 drops substantially.
[02:28] Priya K.: for LumenPay, p99 < 600ms is an internal SLO for our checkout flow. so the 1.2s spikes are outside our comfort.
[02:36] Maya: understood. goal then is to keep throughput high but hit p99 under 600ms. we can aim for two quick experiments: 1) run 20ms window with concurrency 10 and aggressive kv warmup; 2) run 40ms window with misses routed to low-batch pool. compare steady-state for 4 hours.
[02:53] Arjun: sounds good. we also had one anomaly where the queue depth shot up and the runtime started to drop requests - is that expected?
[02:59] Jonah: when queue depth exceeds the configured soft limit the system begins backpressure which can manifest as retries or drop depending on policy. what drop did you see?
[03:07] Daniel: about 0.7% of requests errored during the 40ms run because the client lib retried and then hit a per-route circuit breaker.
[03:15] Sofia: we do have a tight client retry policy so it exacerbated the queue wobble. we can increase the retry backoff but ideally avoid the root cause.
[03:23] Jonah: for the root cause we recommend two changes: tighten queue gating (raise soft cap by 20% so transient spikes don't trip) and enable request shaping per route so high-cost paths get narrower concurrency.
[03:36] Priya R.: can you explain request shaping in plain terms?
[03:39] Jonah: sure. imagine you have two ticket lines: light and heavy. request shaping tunes the number of concurrent tokens each line can consume. heavy routes get a smaller share so they don't starve the rest of the service. it's basically a per-route concurrency quota.
[03:52] Arjun: would shaping affect aggregate throughput? I worry we lose efficiency if we fragment the pool too much.
[03:59] Jonah: small fragmentation often helps. with proper autoscaling and small quotas, the system preserves batching efficiency for the common-case while isolating noisy patterns. we can model it in the lab — we've got a spreadsheet that predicts token/sec under different quotas.
[04:12] Maya: quick interjection — one question you raised earlier about dedicated pools. if you go Dedicated, LumenPay could have isolation and predictable throughput; you'd still get the same runtime features including continuous batching and routing. it's more of a capacity and SLA conversation.
[04:27] Arjun: we are definitely evaluating Dedicated for production if the POC proves out. one reason is regulatory logging and the KMS integration. any difference in latency if we move to dedicated instances?
[04:37] Jonah: negligible difference in base latency; Dedicated just gives you reserved capacity and more deterministic queueing since it's tenant-isolated. sometimes tail improves because there's no noisy neighbor.
[04:46] Sofia: good to know. back to the experiments — Daniel, you mentioned p95 remained okay. do you have SLO burn charts?
[04:53] Daniel: I pulled a small chart. p95 was under 250ms across the runs; p99 only breached when kv miss rate > 10% and we were on 40ms window.
[05:02] Priya K.: what's the plan for warmup script? how many prefixes do we prefetch?
[05:07] Jonah: typical approach is to prefetch top 500 prefixes from your production logs; that covers most of the traffic. we can start with top 200 for the lab. the warmup script will seed the KV with embeddings/hashes and simulate the typical prefix distribution.
[05:20] Arjun: can Redwood provide the warmup script?
[05:23] Maya: yes, Jonah will share it. I'll also attach a short runbook on how to run it in your infra or against Redwood Dedicated.
[05:31] Jonah: one thing to watch for — warmup only helps if the prefix distribution is relatively stable. if product adds dynamic prompts, miss rate creeps up fast.
[05:40] Daniel: we do have a small percentage of dynamic prompts but the checkout flow is quite stable — same templates.
[05:45] Sofia: ok so action items are clear. I'd like to call out observability: we need token-level tracing that ties p99 spikes to either batch composition or kv misses. did you add any new trace id in this run?
[05:58] Jonah: yes we stamped a batch id and kv-hit boolean in the trace. we'll surface a small dashboard that breaks p99 by batch hit vs miss.
[06:07] Priya R.: nice. any anomalies you want to call out?
[06:09] Daniel: one odd thing — during the 40ms run at around 14:20 in the logs there was a short CPU sched hiccup on one node, not sure if it's client-side or infra. we flagged it but it's low frequency.
[06:20] Maya: okay, we'll help triage. could be noise from other background process, but if it recurs we should pin it down.
[06:25] Arjun: what about burst capacity? we have marketing-driven traffic spikes sometimes. if we lock ourselves into low concurrency to meet p99, can we temporarily burst?
[06:34] Jonah: yes, Redwood has burst capacity policies — you can configure reserved baseline and allow bursts with auto-shed/fallback to a cheaper hosted model. For LumenPay, we could set a burst window and fallback rules so critical checkout requests still go through via a smaller, lower-latency path.
[06:49] Priya K.: fallback to a smaller model worries product because quality might change. not ideal for checkout confirmation language.
[06:55] Maya: understood. fallbacks are configurable; you can decide which routes are allowed to fallback and what they return. For example, in a fallback you could return a minimal templated confirmation instead of a generative text.
[07:06] Sofia: that's acceptable for some parts. 
[07:09] Daniel: quick note — we also tried token quantization for a single shard in the lab; it reduced cost by ~20% but increased p95 by 10-15ms. p99 impact was minimal.
[07:20] Jonah: good to know. quantization is a great lever if you can accept small latency and slight quality delta.
[07:26] Arjun: is quantization compatible with KV caching?
[07:29] Jonah: yes, though you must be careful: mixed-precision and cache key equivalence needs to be handled; Redwood runtime supports quantized checkpoints and kv keys are normalized.
[07:38] Priya R.: one procedural question: when we run the 4-hour steady-state, how will Redwood validate the run? what artifacts do you need?
[07:46] Maya: please upload throughput logs (token/sec, batch sizes, batch windows), the trace export with batch ID and kv-hit flags, and a small sample of requests that hit p99. We will ingest and produce a run report.
[07:59] Daniel: okay we'll format logs in the template you shared earlier.
[08:03] Priya K.: timeline — can we have the first run report by Nov 24?
[08:07] Maya: yes, if you run the steady-state by Nov 22 we can have report by Nov 24.
[08:12] Arjun: one last point — security team asked about audit logs and KMS for Dedicated. do you have a SOC2 type doc?
[08:19] Maya: we have SOC2 and ISO docs, plus a KMS integration guide. I'll attach those in the follow-up email.
[08:26] Sofia: perfect. also please include the warmup script and the spreadsheet with the modeled quotas.
[08:31] Jonah: will do. I'll also include a sample config for queue gating and per-route shaping so you can apply it in staging.
[08:40] Daniel: quick nit — when you share the spreadsheet can you add a column for expected cost delta? Product wants to quantify the cost hit for routing misses.
[08:47] Maya: yes we'll add a "cost delta" column and a simple cost calc per 1M tokens.
[08:53] Priya R.: wonderful.
[08:55] -- Recap / Next steps --
[08:56] Maya: recap: Redwood will share (1) perf spreadsheet + cost delta, (2) kv-cache warmup script and runbook, (3) queue gating + shaping sample config, (4) SOC2/KMS docs. LumenPay will run two experiments then a 4-hour steady-state and upload traces.
[09:12] Arjun: agreed. owners: Maya/Jonah and Daniel.
[09:15] Maya: any other questions before we close?
[09:18] Sofia: none from me.
[09:19] Priya K.: none.
[09:20] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll send notes and the artifacts. see you next week same time.

(occasional crosstalk and short filler words removed)
